newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Ekeus fears Iraq trick to hide Scud engines.
newsitem.headline: Ekeus fears Iraq trick to hide Scud engines.

text.p: The United Nations said on Sunday it feared that Iraq was trying to hide operational Scud missile engines by destroying "useless" locally-made ones.

"Iraq (has) produced some home made Scud type engines that were useless but we are afraid they have been mixed into this (1991-92) destruction and high-quality rocket engines were taken out and hidden," said Rolf Ekeus at the end of a Kuwait visit.
"Our idea is to take out these rocket engines to bring them to laboratories for very careful detailed analysis of all components to see how many or if any further (engines) were hidden," he said.

Ekeus, who is on a Gulf Arab tour to raise funds for his commission that is charged with eliminating Iraq's weapons of mass destruction, said U.N. teams were collecting debris earlier this month when "suddenly the Iraqi government blocked us".

He was earlier quoted as saying Iraq's Deputy Prime Minister Tareq Aziz "blocked our team as they were trying to transport the missile parts to our centre in Baghdad after digging them out of the ground...What followed was a rather unpleasant exchange."
A senior U.N. official said last week that the U.N. planned to take the remains of missiles for study outside Iraq to help assess Baghdad's claims that all Scuds had been destroyed.
In 1992 Iraq gave the U.N. a list of hundreds of missiles, launch vehicles and other arms it said it had destroyed and buried in July 1991.
Terms of the ceasefire that ended the 1991 Gulf War over Kuwait ban Iraq from having missiles with a range larger than 150 km (94 miles) and the means to produce them.
Ekeus has said Iraq was still concealing as many as 16 Scuds.
Before leaving for Saudi Arabia, Ekeus warned on Sunday that his commission could be forced to close due to lack of funds.
"We told the (U.N.) Security Council that by the end of the year we are very short, almost all our funds are exhausted and that means we would have to close our operations," he added.
Ekeus said his commission needed $30 million for 1997.
The cash problem is "very sensitive and difficult", said Ekeus, warning that if his commission is closed "there will no longer be any control on Iraq's" military programmes.

Ekeus last year went on a similar Gulf Arab tour ahead of the annual Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) summit to ask for $90 million over three years to finance his commission. This year's GCC summit will be held in Qatar in December.
The last summit said Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Oman and Bahrain would extend political and financial support but did not specify an amount.
